candidates.name: Interference
candidates.quote: The real problem is *interference*: people freeze under pressure, forget the first step, or choose the wrong tool because they misunderstand what the tool is for.
candidates.reason: A core concept explaining the gap between learning and performance, distinct from motivation. It's a specific type of learning failure.

candidates.name: Outcome Ladder
candidates.quote: The Outcome Ladder separates outcomes into four rungs: Rung A: remember (can recall terms) Rung B: recognize (can pick the right option from examples) Rung C: perform (can do the behavior in a realistic scenario) Rung D: transfer (can do it later, in a different context, under stress)
candidates.reason: A defined model for categorizing learning objectives by depth and real-world applicability.

candidates.name: Friction Budget
candidates.quote: Every learning unit has a friction budget: the maximum mental effort a learner can spend before they quit or start guessing.
candidates.reason: A specific concept for managing cognitive load in instructional design, framing effort as a limited resource.

candidates.name: The 7-Minute Microlearning Loop
candidates.quote: Step 1: Choose one Outcome Ladder rung as the target (A, B, C, or D). Step 2: Write one “observable pass condition” (what you can see or measure). Step 3: Create one short scenario with a constraint (time pressure, an annoyed colleague, missing data). Step 4: Offer two actions: the intended action and a tempting wrong action. Step 5: Ask for a choice *and* a one-sentence reason. Step 6: Give feedback in two layers: first a short rule of thumb, then a deeper explanation. Step 7: Add a “next repetition” prompt: when and how to repeat (tomorrow, next meeting, or next real case).
candidates.reason: A complete, step-by-step method for designing an atomic learning unit.

candidates.name: Spend Friction Where It Buys Transfer
candidates.quote: This does not mean “make everything easy.” It means you spend friction where it buys transfer.
candidates.reason: A key design heuristic for applying the Friction Budget concept, guiding where to allocate cognitive effort.

candidates.name: Two-Speed Feedback
candidates.quote: Feedback should come in two speeds. The fast layer is a rule of thumb the learner can remember during a live conversation. The slow layer explains why the rule works and when it fails.
candidates.reason: A specific guideline for structuring feedback to support both immediate recall and deep understanding.

candidates.name: Prefer Fewer, Stronger Links
candidates.quote: Links should point to stable concepts, named models, or repeated prerequisites. Everything else can be left as plain text until it proves useful.
candidates.reason: A rule of thumb for effective linking in a knowledge system, prioritizing quality and utility over quantity.

candidates.name: More Content Means More Learning
candidates.quote: Teams often believe that adding more examples and more theory increases learning. In reality, extra content can raise friction without improving transfer.
candidates.reason: A clearly identified and corrected false belief about instructional design.

candidates.name: Recognition Is Performance
candidates.quote: “If they understood it once, they will perform it later.” Recognition is not performance. People can nod at a good model and still fail under stress.
candidates.reason: A specific, named misconception about the durability of learning, contrasted with the need for transfer.

candidates.name: The Calibration Loop
candidates.quote: A learner calibrates by comparing their choice to an expert choice and understanding the difference. Calibration improves fastest when the learner must commit to a decision before seeing the answer, and when the feedback names the hidden variable.
candidates.reason: A defined process for improving judgment, with specific conditions that accelerate learning.

candidates.name: Manager Scenario: Missing Deadlines
candidates.quote: You are a manager. A team member says: “I keep missing deadlines because other teams block me.” You have two actions: Action A: Ask for a concrete recent example and explore constraints before proposing a solution. Action B: Give advice immediately: “Just communicate earlier and set boundaries.”
candidates.reason: A concrete, illustrative scenario used to demonstrate the application of a coaching principle (diagnostic before advice).

candidates.name: Observable Skill Requirement
candidates.quote: The toolbox above works best when the skill can be observed (even roughly). It can fail when outcomes are invisible or when the environment blocks practice.
candidates.reason: A key boundary condition or guideline for when the microlearning method is applicable.
